etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English beverage, from Old French beverage, variant of bevrage, from beivre (“to drink”), variant of boivre (“to drink”), from Latin bibō. Related to imbibe.

definitions.definition: (chiefly Canada, US) A liquid to consume; a drink, such as tea, coffee, liquor, beer, milk, juice, or a soft drink, usually excluding water.

quote.citation: 1748, James Thomson, “Canto II”, in The Castle of Indolence: […], London:  […]  A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC, stanza VII, page 44:
quote.text: He knew no Beverage but the flowing Stream; / His taſteful well-earn'd Food the ſilvan Game,  […]

quote.citation: 1848, J. S. Skinner & Son, editor, The Plough, The Loom and the Anvil‎[1], volume I, Philadelphia: J. S. Skinner & Son, page 137:
quote.text: [W]here coffee is used as a constant beverage, the gravel and the gout are scarcely known.

definitions.definition: (British, slang, archaic) (A gift of) drink money.
